body:
What are folk and tribal arts?

Folk art refers to artistic traditions developed and practised within communities, often in connection with everyday life, festivals, occupations, marriages and religious observances. These traditions are generally transmitted through families, communities and practical learning rather than through formal art institutions alone.

Tribal art refers to artistic practices associated with particular tribal or Adivasi communities. Its subjects, materials and forms frequently express the community's relationship with nature, ancestors, social customs and religious beliefs.

The categories overlap. Tribal art is often discussed as part of folk art, but every folk tradition is not necessarily tribal. Madhubani painting, for example, is an important regional folk tradition of Bihar, whereas Rathwa Pithora painting is closely associated with a particular tribal community in Gujarat.

Folk art is identified primarily by its community-based cultural tradition. Tribal art is identified more specifically by its association with the traditions of tribal communities. Neither term means that the art lacks skill, refinement or artistic value.

Art as part of community life

Traditional art is not always created merely for decoration. Its meaning often depends on the occasion and the people who make or use it. A painted house wall may form part of a marriage or harvest ceremony. A textile may identify a community or mark the marital status of its wearer. A crafted vessel may be used during worship as well as in ordinary household work.

Consequently, the same object can have several functions:

  • Practical function: a pot stores water, a basket carries grain, and a shawl provides warmth.
  • Ritual function: a painted wall, ceremonial cloth or earthen vessel may be used during worship, marriage or another religious observance.
  • Social function: embroidery, ornaments and garments may indicate community identity, occupation or marital customs.
  • Economic function: the production and sale of craft objects provide income to artisans and their households.
  • Cultural function: motifs and forms preserve stories, beliefs and artistic knowledge across generations.

Why regional forms differ

Artistic traditions develop through interaction between local resources, community beliefs, historical contacts and patterns of patronage. A region with abundant bamboo may develop specialised basketry. Pastoral communities may produce woollen shawls, embroidered garments and animal ornaments. Communities living near clay deposits may specialise in pottery.

Regional identity does not mean complete isolation. Trade, migration, marriage and cultural exchange have continuously influenced Indian crafts. Similar techniques may appear in different states, while a common technique may acquire a distinct local style.

For example, both Gujarat and Rajasthan have important tie-dye traditions. Nevertheless, individual centres such as Jamnagar and Kutch possess recognisable regional products. Similarly, Warli painting is associated especially with Maharashtra, but the geographical area of its registered indication also includes Gujarat and neighbouring territories.

How artistic knowledge is transmitted

Traditionally, many artisans learned by watching and assisting experienced family or community members. Children gradually became familiar with materials, designs, customary uses and the preferences of customers. Some skills were also transmitted through apprenticeship with master craftspersons.

Occupational communities such as Vankars, associated with weaving in Gujarat, and Kumhars or Prajapatis, associated with pottery, illustrate this historical connection between social organisation and specialised craft knowledge.

However, hereditary occupation must not be confused with equal opportunity. Caste restrictions historically limited occupational freedom and social mobility. The preservation of artistic skills occurred alongside these inequalities. Today, training institutions, cooperatives and changing markets allow craft knowledge to circulate beyond its older hereditary boundaries.

Gujarat as an example

Gujarat's folk and craft heritage reflects considerable regional variety. Pithora painting belongs to the ritual traditions of Rathwa communities in eastern Gujarat. Kutch is known for embroidery, Rogan painting, Ajrakh printing and other crafts. Patan is associated with Patola weaving, Jamnagar with Bandhani, and Surendranagar with Tangaliya weaving.

These examples show why an art form should be studied through its region, community, material, method and cultural purpose rather than its name alone.

Prelims focus

  • Folk art is community-based; tribal art has a more specific association with tribal communities.
  • Rathwa communities of eastern Gujarat are associated with Pithora painting.
  • Vankar is a traditional designation associated with weaving.
  • Kumhar or Prajapati is traditionally associated with pottery.
  • Craft objects may have practical, ritual and social functions simultaneously.
  • Trap: Folk and tribal traditions are neither identical categories nor necessarily confined to 1 modern state.

[Sources: NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class XI, 'Crafts Heritage', printed pp. 9–14; NCERT, Craft Traditions of India: Past, Present and Future, Class XII, 'Crafts in the Past', printed pp. 3–10; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class VII, 'The Making of Regional Cultures', printed pp. 122–123; Intellectual Property India, 'State wise Registered GI of India', entries for Warli Painting and Gujarat handicrafts, data as of 31 December 2025, accessed 23 November 2026.]

title: Folk and Tribal Art: Meaning, Community, Ritual and Regional Identity

body:
How to recognise a regional painting tradition

Indian folk and tribal paintings differ in their customary surfaces, subjects, community associations and uses. Some were traditionally painted directly on house walls or floors. Others were created on cloth, paper or portable scrolls.

The material or surface is an important clue, but it is not always decisive. As artists adapted to new markets, several traditions moved from walls and ritual spaces to paper, canvas and other objects. Identification therefore requires more than observing the present-day surface.

Important regional forms

TraditionPrincipal associationCharacteristic subject or context
WarliMaharashtra and adjoining areas, including parts of GujaratGeometrical human and animal figures, village activities, nature and ritual occasions
Madhubani or MithilaMithila region, BiharMarriage and festival paintings, mythological subjects, plants, animals and elaborate patterns
GondGond communities, especially Madhya PradeshAnimals, trees, folklore and forms enriched with lines and dots
BhilBhil communities, especially Madhya Pradesh and RajasthanNature, community beliefs and figures formed through distinctive dotted patterns
PhadRajasthanPainted cloth scrolls associated with the stories of Pabuji and Devnarayan
PattachitraOdisha, especially the Puri regionDevotional and narrative paintings associated with Jagannath traditions
Bengal pata paintingWest BengalNarrative scrolls associated with itinerant singer-painters or patuas

Warli: geometry, nature and community life

Warli painting is an important tribal tradition associated with communities of western India, particularly Maharashtra's northern coastal and adjoining inland regions. Traditional paintings were made on prepared house walls, often using a white pigment derived from rice paste against an earth-coloured background.

Human figures are commonly represented through simple geometrical forms. Circles, triangles and lines combine to depict farming, dancing, animals, plants and other elements of village life.

Warli paintings are also associated with occasions such as marriages and harvest celebrations. The fertility figure Palaghata is an important element of the traditional ritual context.

Although the most familiar geographical association is Maharashtra, the registered geographical indication for Warli Painting covers a wider area that includes Gujarat.

Madhubani: household and ceremonial painting in Bihar

Madhubani painting takes its name from the Madhubani region of Bihar and belongs to the broader cultural area of Mithila. Traditionally, women decorated the walls of their homes, including spaces associated with marriage ceremonies and festivals.

Its subjects include episodes from religious narratives, scenes of nature, animals, plants and auspicious symbols. Dense patterning and the decorative treatment of available space are characteristic of many examples.

Modern Madhubani works are frequently made on paper, cloth and canvas. Their present-day use as marketable paintings does not remove their origin in household and ceremonial traditions.

Gond and Bhil painting

Gond painting draws on the relationship between Gond communities and their natural environment. Animals, birds, trees and folklore are important subjects. Repeated dots, lines and other patterns are used to fill and distinguish forms.

Jangarh Singh Shyam, a Pardhan Gond artist, played an important historical role in bringing Gond imagery into the modern medium of paper and canvas during the 1980s. This is an example of a traditional visual language acquiring new materials and audiences.

Bhil painting is associated especially with Bhil communities of Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan. Its distinctive contemporary vocabulary often employs numerous coloured dots to build images of animals, people, nature and community beliefs.

Both Gond and Bhil painting may employ dots. Their identification must therefore also consider community, themes and overall visual organisation. The presence of dots alone is not sufficient proof of either tradition.

Painted stories on cloth and scrolls

Phad of Rajasthan

Phad is a painted cloth-scroll tradition associated with Rajasthan. It presents the narratives of local heroes and revered figures such as Pabuji and Devnarayan.

The painted scroll traditionally accompanies the narration of these stories by Bhopas. It also functions as a mobile sacred object. Its defining association is therefore not merely cloth painting but a particular tradition of travelling religious and heroic narratives.

Odisha Pattachitra

Pattachitra of Odisha is especially associated with the Puri region and devotional traditions connected with Jagannath. Subjects include religious narratives, including themes from the Gita Govinda. Works may be produced on prepared cloth and other traditional surfaces.

Bengal pata painting

In West Bengal, traditional patuas created painted narrative scrolls and presented stories through song. The visual sequence and the associated oral narrative complemented each other.

The word pata appears in different regional traditions. It does not follow that Bengal's travelling narrative scroll and Odisha's Jagannath-associated Pattachitra are identical practices.

Change within a regional tradition

Traditional painting changes when its makers encounter new audiences, materials and forms of patronage. In colonial Calcutta, for example, Kalighat painting developed as artists adapted earlier village painting practices to a growing urban market. Single-sheet pictures offered a different format from long narrative scrolls.

Similarly, a Gond image on canvas or a Madhubani painting on paper can retain important features of its inherited artistic tradition. A change of surface does not automatically create an entirely new art form.

Prelims focus

  • Warli: geometric figures, ritual wall paintings and village life; principal association with Maharashtra.
  • Madhubani or Mithila: Bihar; household and ceremonial paintings.
  • Gond: central India, especially Madhya Pradesh; Jangarh Singh Shyam is an important modern contributor.
  • Bhil: distinctive dotted painting tradition.
  • Phad: Rajasthan; Pabuji, Devnarayan and Bhopas.
  • Odisha Pattachitra: Puri and Jagannath traditions.
  • Trap: Odisha Pattachitra and Bengal pata painting share a related name but differ in regional and customary context.

[Sources: NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class XI, 'Painting', printed pp. 97–110; NCERT, Craft Traditions of India: Past, Present and Future, Class XII, 'Colonial Rule and Crafts', printed pp. 19–21; Ministry of Tourism, Incredible India, 'Warli Paintings', Maharashtra, accessed 23 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, 'Gond Art: Stories Through Pattern and Colour' and 'Bhil Painting: Stories in Dots and Colours', 2026; Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, 'Phad: Scroll Paintings and Their Narration, Rajasthan', Intangible Cultural Heritage inventory; Los Angeles County Museum of Art, collection note on Jangarh Singh Shyam; Intellectual Property India, state-wise GI register, Warli Painting, application 239, data as of 31 December 2025.]
title: Major Folk and Tribal Painting Traditions of India

body:
Pithora: a ritual wall-painting tradition

Pithora painting is closely associated with the Rathwa community of eastern Gujarat, especially the Chhota Udepur region. It is also practised in related tribal cultural areas beyond Gujarat.

Traditional Pithora paintings are made on the walls of houses in connection with religious beliefs and community observances. They are not simply pictures selected to decorate a room. The occasion, the subject matter and the involvement of the household are part of the significance of the work.

Paintings contain horses, human figures, animals and other elements from the community's religious and social world. The prominent representation of horses is an important recognition clue.

The traditional painter is known as a Lakhara. The painting belongs to a larger ritual setting involving the household and its customs.

Pithora demonstrates how a visual art can preserve community memory while serving a specific ceremonial purpose.

Pithora is associated with Rathwa communities, ritual house-wall painting and the Chhota Udepur region. It is a registered geographical indication of Gujarat, application number 644.

Mata ni Pachhedi: a sacred painted textile

Mata ni Pachhedi is a traditional painted and block-printed cloth associated particularly with Ahmedabad and the Vaghari or Devi-Pujak community.

The name refers to the cloth placed behind the mother goddess. A related cloth canopy is known as Mata no Chandarvo. These textiles have been used to create or furnish temporary religious spaces.

Traditional examples often use black, maroon or red and other limited colours. They depict mother-goddess traditions and associated narrative or decorative elements. The craft combines painting and block printing on cloth.

Members of the community who make these works are traditionally referred to as Chitaras, or painters.

The important distinction is that Mata ni Pachhedi is a painted ritual textile, not a woven picture or an embroidered wall hanging. Its religious function also explains why its traditional format differs from an ordinary decorative fabric.

Rogan: oil-based painting on fabric

Rogan painting is particularly associated with Nirona village in Kutch. It is a textile-painting craft, rather than a method of weaving patterns into fabric.

Traditional Rogan work uses a thick, paint-like substance prepared from processed castor oil mixed with pigments. The artist develops ornamental designs on cloth with a metal implement.

The Tree of Life is a well-known motif of the Nirona tradition. Floral and other ornamental designs are also characteristic.

Rogan-painted textiles have been used in clothing and decorative objects and are now also made for wider craft markets.

The name's association with oil is important: Rogan is not another name for Bandhani, Ajrakh or embroidery. The distinguishing element is the use of a specially prepared, oil-based painting medium on the fabric.

Pithora is primarily identified by its ritual wall-painting tradition. Mata ni Pachhedi is a painted devotional cloth. Rogan is identified by oil-based ornamental painting on fabric.

Other related traditions in Gujarat

Warli painting is also found among communities in southern Gujarat. Its broader regional distribution is an example of cultural traditions crossing present-day state boundaries.

Lippan work, associated with Kutch, combines mud or clay-based relief decoration with small mirrors on walls. It is different from mirror embroidery and from Pithora's ritual narrative wall painting.

Gujarat's painting traditions therefore cannot be classified adequately by the single fact that they use colour. Their differences lie in the surface, material, cultural purpose and artistic method.

Why these distinctions matter

Consider a painted cloth used behind a mother-goddess shrine in Ahmedabad. Its religious setting and textile surface point to Mata ni Pachhedi. A house-wall painting of horses associated with the Rathwa community points to Pithora. An ornamental Tree of Life made with castor-oil-based pigment on cloth in Nirona points to Rogan.

These are not merely 3 alternative names for Gujarat painting. Each refers to a distinct regional craft tradition.

Prelims focus

  • Pithora: Rathwa community, Chhota Udepur, ritual wall painting.
  • Lakhara: traditional painter associated with Pithora.
  • Mata ni Pachhedi: Ahmedabad, Vaghari or Devi-Pujak community, sacred painted cloth.
  • Mata no Chandarvo: related ceremonial cloth canopy.
  • Rogan: Nirona, Kutch; castor-oil-based textile painting; Tree of Life motif.
  • Trap: Rogan is painted on cloth; it is neither an ikat weave nor a form of embroidered mirror work.

[Sources: Ministry of Tourism, Incredible India, 'Pithora: The Enigmatic Ritual of Pithora Paintings', section on Rathwa community and Lakhara painters, accessed 23 November 2026; Sandeep Joshi, 'Kalamkari of Gujarat: Mata ni Pachhedi', Sahapedia, sections 'Introduction' and 'The Vaghri Community', accessed 23 November 2026; Ministry of Tourism, Incredible India, 'Visit Nirona in Kutch', sections 'Rogan Art' and 'Preserving an Identity', accessed 23 November 2026; Gujarat Tourism, 'Niche Tourism', Art and Craft listings, accessed 23 November 2026; Intellectual Property India, state-wise registered GI list, applications 644, 694 and 718, data as of 31 December 2025.]
